lesson.title: Rules for 2, 5 and 10
lesson.body: Look at the last digit. A number divides by 2 when it ends in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8; by 5 when it ends in 0 or 5; by 10 when it ends in 0.

lesson.title: Rules for 4, 8, 11 and 12
lesson.body: 4: the last two digits divide by 4. 8: the last three digits divide by 8. 11: the sums of alternate digits are equal or differ by 11. 12: it divides by both 3 and 4.

lesson.title: Prime or composite
lesson.body: A prime number has exactly two factors, 1 and itself: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13. A composite number has more, like 12 = 3 × 4. 1 is neither.

lesson.title: Prime factorisation
lesson.body: Divide by primes until only primes are left: 72 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 = 2³ × 3². Every number above 1 has exactly one prime factorisation.

lesson.title: The GCF
lesson.body: The GCF of 12 and 18 is the biggest number that divides both: 6. List the factors of each, or use prime factors: 12 = 2 × 2 × 3 and 18 = 2 × 3 × 3 share 2 × 3 = 6.

lesson.title: Continuous division
lesson.body: Divide both numbers by a prime they share, again and again: 12 and 18 ÷ 2 gives 6 and 9; ÷ 3 gives 2 and 3, which share nothing. Multiply the primes you used: 2 × 3 = 6.

lesson.title: The LCM
lesson.body: The LCM of 4 and 6 is the smallest number both divide into: 12. List the multiples: 4, 8, 12 and 6, 12. The first one in both lists is the LCM.

lesson.title: GCF or LCM?
lesson.body: Sharing things into the most equal groups: the GCF. Things that repeat and meet again, like buses or visits: the LCM.

templates.construct: Solve a sharing problem with the GCF

formats.prompt: Ana has {a} red beads and {b} blue beads. She makes bracelets that are all the same and uses every bead. What is the greatest number of bracelets she can make?
{a} boys and {b} girls are put into teams. Every team has the same number of boys and the same number of girls, and everyone is in a team. What is the greatest number of teams?

hints: The number of groups must divide both {a} and {b}: it is a common factor.
The greatest number of groups is the GCF of {a} and {b}.
steps: The groups divide both {a} and {b} exactly
So the number of groups is a common factor; the most is the GCF
templates.explain: The GCF of {a} and {b} is {answer}, so {answer} groups, each with {x} and {y}.

distractors.feedback: {value} is the LCM. Sharing into equal groups uses the GCF, the biggest number that divides both.
{value} is how many are in each group. The question asks how many groups.

templates.construct: Solve a meeting-again problem with the LCM

hints: They meet again at a number both {a} and {b} divide into: a common multiple.
The next time is the least common multiple.
steps: Both repeat, so they meet at common multiples of {a} and {b}
The first time is the LCM

templates.construct: Find how many packs make two pack sizes come out even, with the LCM

formats.prompt: Hotdogs come in packs of {a} and buns in packs of {b}. Kiko wants exactly one bun for each hotdog, with none left over. What is the least number of packs of buns he can buy?
Pencils come in packs of {a} and erasers in packs of {b}. Teacher Ana wants the same number of pencils and erasers. What is the least number of packs of erasers she can buy?

hints: The total must be a multiple of both {a} and {b}: a common multiple.
The least one is the LCM: {a} = {g} × {x} and {b} = {g} × {y}, so the LCM is {g} × {x} × {y} = {g * x * y}.
How many packs of {b} make {g * x * y}?
templates.explain: The least total both pack sizes make is the LCM, {g * x * y}, and {g * x * y} ÷ {b} = {answer} packs of {b}.

distractors.feedback: {value} is how many items: the LCM. Each pack holds {b}, so divide: {value} ÷ {b}.
{value} packs of {a} make the LCM. The question asks for packs of {b}.
{value} packs of {b} work too, but they are not the least: {value} × {b} = {a * b}, and the LCM is only {g * x * y}.
